rv.q: It’s perhaps the first time in my life that I’ve been happy to see a confetti cannon at curtain call.

“The Heart of Rock and Roll,” which does not look like it cost $30 million and is all the better for that, feels happy to play to its target audience of Huey fans who prefer a decent beer to Moët & Chandon any night of the week.
The jukebox musical 'The Heart of Rock & Roll,' built around the hits of Huey Lewis and the News, is energetic and well-performed but feels more like a concert than a cohesive story.

For all the familiar jukebox musical templates of thin characters, unsurprising plot developments and oldie pop/rock songs shoehorned into the narrative, there's something to be said for simple packaging that knows what it is and does it well.
In the moment, it’s easy to laugh along with The Heart of Rock and Roll’s relentless charm offensive.
But too often, book writer Jonathan A. Abrams and director Gordon Greenberg are content to get laughs by deploying reliable cultural stereotypes
That’s the only explanation for a show as rote and paint-by-numbers predictable as “The Heart of Rock and Roll.”
The heart of rock and roll is still beating.

As with his recent Broadway success, “Gutenberg!,” director Gordon Greenberg takes his job seriously, keeping the show moving as a fleet pace. Better still, he also never makes the show too serious, ensuring that its tongue remains firmly planted in one cheek or another almost the whole time.
Even if you’re not an admirer, “The Heart of Rock and Roll” offers more zany grace and buoyancy than most of its peers.
I came out feeling buzzed, entertained…and slightly ashamed at how easily I swallowed this package.
Fortunately the music is so damn infectious and the story so playfully silly, it hardly matters.
Director Gordon Greenberg's production is eager to sweep you up in its bright lights
But for what it is, the show has its moments.
The Heart of Rock and Roll formula feels phony and forced, but if you don't find fun in the familiar, you may discover some moving moments through its fringe characters.
Outside of that enjoyable kooky detour, the show mostly plods through its confounding second act, weighed down by the essential strangeness of Bobby’s narrative dilemma.
Gordon Greenberg directs and Lorin Latarro choreographs, achieving some kind of immortality with all that bubble wrap. Around the edges of this production are a few inspired performances. Raymond J.
Heart does has heart in the sense that all involved perform at a professional level, but the show’s vital organ is a recycled, synthetic one.

This show delivers on the promise of its seemingly generic title — there’s plenty of heart as well as rock and roll — and it’s performed with energy, intelligence, and an absolute commitment to entertain.
This show takes classic, well-loved, music and asks us to simply have a good time, which I argue is a goal they overwhelmingly accomplished.
Overall, “The Heart of Rock and Roll” is a feel-good, sweet, and fun show, filled with much levity.

cn.t: This Huey Lewis jukebox musical earns mixed-to-positive reviews for its unpretentious fun and catchy '80s nostalgia, though critics note its thin plot and familiar formula. Most find it a surprisingly enjoyable crowd-pleaser.

sg.ra: JEJ is one of Broadway's smallest houses (1,063-1,092 seats across sources) and seats 101-112 in Center Orch rows AA-A put you almost nose-to-stage; SeatPlan and Headout both name seats 105-109 in AA-A as the single best spots. Mezz overhang doesn't bite until Row J, so Center Orch stays clean of ceiling cutoff all the way back to Row I.

SeatPlan explicitly calls out 'Rows E to J in the Center Orchestra are cheaper than premium with a good view,' and because JEJ's auditorium is unusually compact even Row J sits closer to the stage than mid-orch in bigger Shubert houses. This is the sweet spot before the Mezz overhang obscures the top of the stage (SeatPlan: cuts in after Row O; TickPick: overhang begins Row J but worsens deeper).

sg.vl: Overview pick with an elevated head-on
sg.ra: JEJ Mezz is one of Broadway's smallest (264-275 seats) and sits directly above the stage per SeatPlan: 'every row facing directly above the stage.' SeatPlan notes the Balcony overhang at Mezz Row B 'doesn't affect views' and the railing height doesn't obstruct (TickPick). Good rake means heads-in-front is a non-issue. AVFMS April 2024: 'View was fantastic, person in front didn't obstruct my view.'

sg.vl: Underrated value if you skew center
sg.ra: Unusual for Broadway, TickPick explicitly states JEJ 'does not have obstructed view seats on the sides of the orchestra and mezzanine' thanks to the small footprint and no pillars. But SeatPlan warns double-digit seats at the far side and Boxes above 16 are angled with stage right partially obstructed, so you want the low-numbered seats closer to center aisle.
sg.rr: L Mezz A-G odd 1-25; R Mezz A-G even 2-26; plus 24 box seats

sg.vl: Cheapest tier, steepest price in comfort
sg.ra: SeatPlan: Balcony is 'very steep and cramped compared to the lower two seating areas,' ~2 steps down per row with three flights of stairs (Shubert: 55 steps total or elevator post-renovation). SeatPlan flags Row H as 'isn't as well-raked as the rest of the section,' so the back row both loses rake AND inherits the steep climb. JEJ balcony is unusually high — Shubert's own description puts it behind Row F entrance.
sg.rr: A-G (L/R) / A-H (Center); 283 seats plus 12 box seats

vr.q: I just genuinely love this show. I think it is so fun and goofy and filled with incredibly talented people.
I don't think I've had this much fun watching a show in a really, really long time.
if you're just looking for a fun night out at the theater, this is honestly a pretty good option.
